paragraphs.text: The festive consumption of food and drink was an important social ritual in the Roman world. The Romans distinguished between specific types of gatherings, such as the public banquet and the dinner served punctually midday through the afternoon in private houses. Public banquets, such as the civic feasts offered to all of the inhabitants of a city, often accommodated large numbers of diners. In contrast, the dinner parties that took place in residences were more private affairs in which the host entertained a small group of family friends, business associates and clients.

Roman literary sources are united in describing elite private dinners as a kind of feast for the senses, during which the host strove to impress his guests with extravagant food, luxurious tableware and diverse forms of entertainment, all of which were enjoyed in a lavishly adorned setting. Archaeological evidence of Roman housing has shed important light on the contexts in which private dinners occurred, and on the types of objects employed during such gatherings.

The dining room was one of the most important reception spaces of the residence and, as such, it included high-quality decorative fixtures, such as floor mosaics and wall paintings, as well as portable luxury objects, such as sculptures and furniture.

The Romans reclined on couches while eating. A dining room typically held three broad couches, each of which seated three individuals, thus allowing for a total of nine guests. This type of room is commonly described as a ‘three-couch room’. The couches were arranged along three walls of the room, at the centre of which was placed a table that was accessible to all of the diners. Couches were frequently made of wood, but there were also more opulent versions with fittings made of costly materials, such as ivory and bronze.

A proper Roman dinner included three courses: starter, main course and dessert usually involving ingredients like fruit and honey. The food that was served was intended not only to fill the guests’ stomachs, but also to add an element of spectacle to the meal. Exotic produce, particularly that from wild animals, birds, and fish, was favoured at elite dinner parties because of its rarity, difficulty of procurement and consequent high cost, which reflected the host’s affluence. Popular but costly food items included pheasant, songbirds, raw oysters, lobster, shellfish, venison, wild boar, and peacock. Recipes were invented, often requiring not only expensive ingredients and ways of cooking, but also dramatic forms of presentation. For example, in the fictional Trimalchio’s Dinner, written between 54 and 68 AD, Trimalchio serves his guests numerous extravagant dishes, such as a hare decorated with wings to resemble the mythological winged horse Pegasus.

Such a meal required a table service comprising numerous vessels and utensils that were designed to serve both functional and decorative purposes. The most expensive tableware was made of costly materials, such as silver, gold, bronze, or semi-precious stones. However, even a family of moderate means would likely have owned a set of table silver.

A complete table service included silver for both eating and drinking. Silver for food included large serving trays and dishes, as well as individual bowls and plates, as well as spoons, which were the primary eating utensil used by the Romans. Knives and forks were less commonly used, although examples have survived. Among the drinking silver, cups came in a variety of forms, the most popular of which were two-handled drinking cups. These were often decorated with naturalistic plants, animals and mythological subjects.

Similar types of tableware were also made of less costly materials, yet they exhibit a high level of craftsmanship. Glass had become especially fashionable and was more readily available in the Roman world following the rapid development of its manufacture in the first half of the first century AD.

Affordable containers for liquids could also be made of a cheap form of pottery. These were produced in various parts of the Roman empire, particularly in present-day France, where such plain and decorated vessels were mass-produced and exported to different parts of the empire.

The final component of the dinner was its entertainment, which was designed to delight both the eye and ear. Musical performances often involved the flute, the water-organ, and the lyre, as well as choral works. Active forms of entertainment could include troupes of acrobats, dancers, gladiators, mime, pantomime and even trained animals, such as lions and leopards. There were also gentler options, such as recitations of poetry, histories, and dramatic performances. Even the staff and slaves of the house were incorporated into the entertainment: singing cooks performed as they served guests.

In conclusion, the Roman dinner was not merely a meal but rather a calculated spectacle that was intended to demonstrate to guests that the host was wealthy and sophisticated. At the same time, the host hoped to outdo the lavish dinners of his friends and colleagues.
